title: Friction & Circular Motion
summary: Friction opposes sliding, $f=\mu N$, with static friction up to a maximum before slipping. Uniform circular motion requires a centripetal (inward) force $F_c=mv^2/r$, supplied by friction, tension, gravity, or a banked road.

static friction.plain: Friction preventing sliding, up to a max.

centripetal force.plain: Net inward force for circular motion.

banked curve.in_class: The normal force's component turns the car.

concept_sections.heading: Kinetic friction
concept_sections.explanation: While an object slides, kinetic friction opposes the motion with magnitude $f_k=\mu_k N$. Include it in the force balance along the surface.

concept_sections.heading: Static friction
concept_sections.explanation: Static friction adjusts to prevent sliding up to a maximum $f_{s,\max}=\mu_s N$. An object stays put until the applied force exceeds this.
math_steps: Static friction matches the applied force.

concept_sections.heading: Centripetal acceleration
concept_sections.explanation: An object moving in a circle at constant speed accelerates toward the center: $a_c=v^2/r$. Its velocity direction constantly changes.
math_steps: It needs a net inward force.

concept_sections.heading: Centripetal force
concept_sections.explanation: Some real force must provide the inward pull: $F_c=mv^2/r$. Identify it (friction, tension, gravity) and set it equal to $mv^2/r$.

concept_sections.heading: Cars on curves
concept_sections.explanation: On a flat curve, static friction supplies the centripetal force, giving a maximum safe speed $v=\sqrt{\mu_s g r}$; banking lets a road turn cars with less reliance on friction.

real_world_examples.title: Anti-lock brakes
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: They keep tires in static (not kinetic) friction, which grips better for shorter stops.

real_world_examples.title: A car on a highway ramp
real_world_examples.scenario: A curved ramp turns a car.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Friction (or banking) supplies $mv^2/r$; exceed the max speed and it skids.

real_world_examples.title: A spinning bucket of water
real_world_examples.scenario: Water stays in an over-the-top swing.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The required centripetal force keeps the water pressed inward at the top.
